extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers in geometric analysis and Ricci flow (study of Perelman's work)
extracted.subtask_description: Precise criteria and structural theorems describing local and singularity geometry for Ricci flow on compact orientable three-manifolds (canonical neighborhoods, pinching, noncollapsing, curvature estimates). Useful for identifying when a region is close to an ancient κ-solution and for obtaining curvature/volume bounds used in surgery/long-time analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalized initial metric
rubrics_metrics.description: A Riemannian metric on a compact orientable three-manifold is normalized if the eigenvalues of its curvature operator at every point are bounded by 1/10, and every geodesic ball of radius one has volume at least one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normalization is used as a uniform initial condition so the evolution has controlled pinching and allows rescaling arguments; one may rescale any initial metric to satisfy this normalization before applying the subsequent theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pinching estimate for solutions with normalized initial metric (equations (7.1.1)-(7.1.2))
rubrics_metrics.description: For a solution gij(x,t) to the Ricci flow with normalized initial metric on a compact three-manifold, there is a pinching estimate of the form Rm(x,t) ≥ -[f^{-1}(R(1+t))/(R(1+t))] R(x,t) (equation (7.1.1)), equivalently Rm(x,t) ≥ -[f^{-1}(R(1+t))/(R(1+t))] R(x,t) (rewritten in (7.1.2)), where f(x)=x(log x - 3) is increasing/convex and f^{-1}(y)/y → 0 as y→∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This quantitative curvature-pinching controls negative part of curvature operator in terms of scalar curvature and is used repeatedly in taking limits and applying maximum principles; it justifies that high-scalar-curvature regions are nearly nonnegative-curvature when rescaled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical Neighborhood Theorem (Theorem 6.4.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any ε>0 there exist positive constants C1(ε), C2(ε) such that for any three-dimensional nonflat (compact or noncompact) ancient κ-solution (M,g(t)), either the solution is the round RP^2×R, or every point (x,t) has an open neighborhood B = Bt(x,r) (with Bt(x,2r) ⊂ B_t(x,2r) for some 0<r<C1 R(x,t)^{-1/2}) which falls into one of three categories: (a) an evolving ε-neck (after scaling by R(x,t) and shifting time to 0, ε-close in C^[ε^{-1}] topology to a subset of the evolving standard round cylinder S^2×R of scalar curvature 1); (b) an evolving ε-cap (time-slice at t of an evolving metric on B^3 or RP^3 outside a compact subset, matched to an evolving ε-neck); (c) a compact manifold without boundary with positive sectional curvature (thus diffeomorphic to S^3 or a metric quotient). Additionally, scalar curvature on B is between C2^{-1} R(x,t) and C2 R(x,t), and in cases (a) & (b) the volume satisfies (C2 R(x,t))^{-3/2} ≤ Vol_t(B) ≤ ε r^3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the canonical neighborhood classification used to recognize local geometry at high-curvature points: roughly necks, caps, or positively curved compact pieces, with precise curvature and volume control and C^{[ε^{-1}]} closeness after the natural rescaling.

rubrics_metrics.name: κ-noncollapsing on bounded scales (used repeatedly)
rubrics_metrics.description: For solutions with normalized initial metric (and in particular for limits obtained by the rescaling arguments used here) there exists κ>0 (depending only on T0 or normalization) such that the solution is κ-noncollapsed on all scales less than √T0 (or on all relevant scales after rescaling).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Noncollapsing is required to apply Hamilton compactness and to extract nonflat limits; it underlies the ability to control injectivity radii and obtain C∞loc convergence of rescaled solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Singularity structure theorem (Theorem 7.1.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given ε>0 and T0>1 there exists r0>0 such that: if gij(x,t) is a solution on a compact orientable three-manifold with normalized initial metric defined on [0,T) with 1<T≤T0, then for any point (x0,t0) with t0≥1 and Q = R(x0,t0) ≥ 1, the solution in the parabolic region { (x,t) | d_{t0}^2(x,x0) < r0^2 Q^{-1}, t0 - r0^2 Q^{-1} ≤ t ≤ t0 } is, after scaling by factor Q, ε-close in the C^{[ε^{-1}]} topology to the corresponding subset of some orientable ancient κ-solution (for some κ>0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides the precise criterion to identify high-curvature parabolic neighborhoods as modeled by ancient κ-solutions after the natural parabolic rescaling; r0 depends only on ε and T0. It is the main tool to transfer canonical neighborhood structure from ancient solutions to finite-time singular regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local curvature derivative bounds / local curvature control (Lemma 7.1.2 and its use)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a space-time point lies in a region that is ε-close to an ancient κ-solution (as in the previous theorems) then one obtains local curvature bounds and derivative estimates: on suitable short parabolic segments where scalar curvature is ≥ 2Q_k one has control of spatial and time derivatives of curvature (estimates of the form |∇R| ≤ const·R^{3/2}, |∂R/∂t| ≤ const·R^2 after rescaling). Integrating these derivative estimates along suitable curves yields local upper bounds on curvature on small parabolic neighborhoods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemma 7.1.2 is used to extend pointwise high-curvature information to uniform control on nearby space-time regions and to prevent sudden blow-up away from chosen basepoints; its conclusion is crucial for applying Hamilton compactness and Shi estimates to take limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curvature boundedness at bounded distance after rescaling (Claim/Step 2 in proof of Thm 7.1.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each finite A there exists C(A) such that for the rescaled solutions around points (x_k,t_k) (scaled so R(x_k,t_k)=1), the scalar curvature ˜R_k(y,0) ≤ C(A) for all y with d_{˜g_k}(y,x_k) ≤ A. Equivalently: after appropriate rescaling, curvature is uniformly bounded on any fixed radius ball around basepoints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is proved by contradiction using the canonical neighborhood classification, geodesic-segment arguments, and nonnegativity/pinching; it yields precompactness (with κ-noncollapsing) needed to extract a nonflat limit ancient κ-solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounded curvature of the limit and backward extension (Steps 3–4 in proof of Thm 7.1.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any C∞loc limit obtained by the rescalings above has nonnegative curvature operator, bounded curvature on each time-slice, and in fact the limit extends backwards in time (to a maximal interval (t',0]) with bounded curvature on each slice). If curvature were unbounded at time-slices or as t→t' one derives contradictions (splitting, neck analysis) that force the limit to be an ancient κ-solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These structural continuity/extension properties are used to conclude the rescaled limit is an ancient κ-solution (contradicting the assumed failure of the theorem) and rely on Li–Yau–Hamilton estimates, maximum principles, and Lemma 7.1.2 to prevent pathological blow-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elliptic-type curvature estimate via volume (Perelman's theorem 7.2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any A<∞ there exist constants K=K(A) and α=α(A)>0 such that: if a solution to Ricci flow on a compact orientable three-manifold with normalized initial metric satisfies for some x0 and some r0>0 with r0<α that the solution is defined for 0≤t≤r0^2, Rm(x,t) ≤ 2 r0^{-2} for 0≤t≤r0^2 and d0(x,x0)<r0, and Vol_0(B_0(x0,r0)) ≥ A^{-1} r0^3, then R(x,r0^2) ≤ K r0^{-2} whenever d_{r0^2}(x,x0) < A r0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a scale-invariant curvature bound at time r0^2 under a uniform initial local volume lower bound and a modest prior curvature bound on the space-time region. The proof uses Perelman's no local collapsing II, the singularity structure theorem, rescaling/compactness, and the claim that failure implies existence of ε-close ancient κ-solutions which leads to contradiction. The theorem is a key tool to control curvature by initial volume and local geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dichotomy used in proofs: either curvature bound or ε-close to ancient κ-solution (auxiliary claim in Theorem 7.2.1 proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the hypotheses used in the proof (normalized initial metric, initial local curvature bound Rm ≤ 2 r0^{-2} on a parabolic region and uniform local volume lower bound), for any fixed ε>0 one can find K such that for any point x with appropriate bounds either R(x,r0^2) < K r0^{-2} or the parabolic neighborhood around (x,r0^2) (after scaling by R(x,r0^2)) is ε-close to the corresponding subset of an orientable ancient κ-solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This dichotomy is the engine in the bootstrap argument: if a region is not controlled by K then it must be modeled by an ancient κ-solution, and that modeling leads to contradictions (via earlier canonical neighborhood/neck/cap analysis) unless the curvature is actually bounded. The claim is proved by adjusting basepoints and iterative rescaling as in the singularity structure theorem.
